v: Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
o: Every new beginning starts in a place that does not look like a beginning at all.
w: Find something small that is alive and growing: a houseplant, a tree outside your window, a single flower from the grocery store. Put it where you will see it every day this month. Let it be your reminder that new things spring forth quietly.

t: The Substance of Things Hoped For
v: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
o: We often talk about faith as if it were a feeling, something light and airy that floats in when we are inspired and drifts away when we are tired. But the writer of Hebrews uses two very solid words to describe it: substance and evidence.
w: Write down one thing you are hoping for that you cannot yet see. Fold the paper and tuck it inside the back cover of this book. On Day 30, you will open it again.

v: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
o: There is a word in this verse that I love: present.
w: Choose a moment today when you would normally reach for your phone to fill the silence. Instead, sit still for three full minutes. Breathe slowly and repeat one phrase: God is present.

v: It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
o: It surprises many people to learn where this beloved verse comes from. It is not found in a book of celebration. It is found in Lamentations, a book of grief, written in the ashes of a ruined city.
w: Tomorrow morning, before you look at your phone or your to-do list, say out loud: Your mercies are new this morning. Then name one specific mercy you can see, however small.

v: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
o: Faith is not only for the days when the answer is clear. It is for the mornings when you pray and still have to wait, and you choose to trust God in the waiting.
w: Take a slow, intentional walk today, even ten minutes around your block or your workplace. As you walk, pray about the thing you are waiting for. Let each step be a small act of trust.

t: When You Cannot See the Path
v: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
o: Many of us are very good at understanding. We are planners, organisers, problem-solvers. We are the ones others call when something needs to be handled. Those are real gifts, and God uses them.
w: Write down a situation where you have been leaning hard on your own understanding. Beside it, write one faithful next step. Only one. Take that step today.

v: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
o: This may be the most honest prayer in the whole Bible.
w: Write your doubts down plainly in your journal, without softening them. Then write the father's prayer beneath them. Hand both to God.

v: For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
o: Weeping may endure for a night.
w: If you can, watch a sunrise this week. If not, simply notice the light the next time you wake. Thank God out loud for one sign that morning is coming in your life.

v: We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed.
o: Paul does not pretend in this passage. He does not tell us that faithful people avoid trouble. He lists it plainly: troubled on every side, perplexed, persecuted, cast down. If you have ever felt pressed from every direction at once, Paul understands.
w: Make a short list titled But Not. For each hard thing you are facing, write the hard thing, then write the word but, and finish the sentence with a truth from today's verse.

v: Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.
o: Ruth's story begins in grief. Her husband has died. Her father-in-law has died. Her brother-in-law has died. Three widows stand together on a road, and the oldest of them, Naomi, tells the younger two to go home and start again.
w: Identify one unglamorous, faithful task you have been putting off because it feels too small to matter. Do it today, and offer it to God as an act of staying.

v: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
o: Joseph had every reason to be bitter.
w: Write two columns. In the first, honestly name something that was meant for harm in your life. In the second, write any way, however small, that God has already begun to bring good from it. If the second column is empty, write: Not yet, but God.

t: When I Fall, I Shall Arise
v: Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
o: Notice the prophet does not say if I fall. He says when.
w: Think of a recent fall, a mistake, a harsh word, a broken commitment. Take one concrete step to rise from it today: an apology, a fresh start, or simply a decision to stop replaying it.

v: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
o: Paul had something he called a thorn in the flesh. We do not know exactly what it was. Scholars have guessed at an illness, a disability, a persistent opponent. Paul does not tell us, and perhaps that is a gift, because it lets each of us read our own thorn into his story.
w: Name your thorn honestly. Then write: Your grace is sufficient for me in this. Read it aloud each time the thorn makes itself felt today.

v: And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
o: There is a particular kind of tiredness that comes from doing the right thing for a long time without seeing results.
w: Plant something this week: a seed in a cup, a bulb in the garden, a few herbs on a windowsill. Water it and watch it. Let it teach you about due seasons.

v: And the angel of the LORD came again the second time, and touched him, and said, Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee.
o: Elijah had just experienced one of the greatest victories in Scripture. On Mount Carmel, fire fell from heaven and God proved Himself before a whole nation. And immediately afterward, Elijah ran for his life, sat down under a juniper tree, and asked God to let him die.
w: Plan one act of real rest this week, and put it on your calendar as seriously as any appointment: a nap, a quiet meal, an evening with no obligations. Do not apologise for it.

v: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
o: Just after this verse, the psalmist says something that seems almost out of place. He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.
w: Find a quiet place, open your hands on your lap, and tell God about one wound you have been carrying. Speak it out loud if you can. Then sit in silence for a few minutes and let Him be near.

v: And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.
o: For twelve years, she had been bleeding.
w: Write the word Daughter at the top of a page. Beneath it, write every name you have called yourself in your lowest seasons. Then draw a single line through each one.

v: And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?
o: Hagar was a woman with almost no power over her own life.
w: Find a place near water today, even a glass of water on your kitchen table. Sit with it and say Hagar's words: You are the God who sees me.

v: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
o: Some of us were taught that grief is something to get over. We were given a few days, maybe a few weeks, and then we were expected to be fine. We learned to say I'm okay when we were not okay, because it was easier than explaining that the loss still hurt.
w: Make a list of the losses you have not fully grieved. Choose one and do something to honour it: write a letter, visit a meaningful place, or simply speak its name to God.

v: To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
o: In the ancient world, people in mourning would sit in ashes and sometimes put ashes on their heads. It was an outward sign of inward devastation. Everything has burned, the ashes said. Nothing is left.
w: Write down one area of your life that still feels like ashes. Hold the paper in your open hands and pray: Lord, I am ready for the exchange. Then put it somewhere you will see it again on Day 30.

v: Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
o: Forgiveness may be the hardest part of healing, and it is also one of the most misunderstood.
w: Write the name of one person you need to forgive, even if that person is you. Beneath it, write: I release this debt to God. You do not need to send it or tell anyone. This is between you and God.

v: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
o: Butterflies appear on the covers of both of my books for a reason. There is no better picture of transformation in all of creation.
w: Look up a short video of a butterfly emerging from its chrysalis and watch it slowly. Then write one sentence describing who you are becoming.

v: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
o: This is one of the most quoted verses in the Bible. It appears on graduation cards and wall plaques and coffee mugs. But it helps to remember who first received it.
w: Ask yourself: if I knew this season would last a long time, what would I build here? What would I plant? Choose one thing and begin it this week.

t: For Such a Time as This
v: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
o: Esther's life did not begin in a palace. She was an orphan, raised by her cousin Mordecai, a member of a minority people living in exile. Through a series of events she did not choose, she ended up as queen of Persia.
w: Make a list of the places where you have influence: your workplace, your church, your family, your community, your online circles. Pray over each one and ask: Why might I be here, for such a time as this?

v: Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
o: This verse answers one of the deepest questions a hurting heart can ask: What good can possibly come from my pain?
w: Think of someone who is walking through something you have survived. Reach out to them this week with a simple message: I have been thinking about you. I have walked a similar road. I am here.

v: Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?
o: She came to the well at noon, in the heat of the day, when no one else would be there.
w: Write your testimony in three short paragraphs: Before, Encounter, and After. Keep it honest and simple. You do not need to share it yet. Just write it.

v: And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
o: This verse speaks to anyone who has ever carried a vision, and it speaks to me as a writer.
w: Write your vision. Give it a full page. Describe the life, the work, or the purpose you sense God calling you toward, in plain words. Date it and keep it.

v: Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
o: After a painful season, many of us pull back from people. We have been hurt, so we decide it is safer to rely on no one. We become fiercely independent. We tell ourselves we do not need anyone.
w: Invite one woman to walk through this book with you, or simply to share a meal. Be honest with her about one thing you have been carrying alone.

t: He Will Finish What He Started
v: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.
o: As we near the end of these thirty days, I want to remind you of something important. This book is ending, but God's work in you is not.
w: Look back through your journal from these four weeks. Underline one sentence from each week that shows growth, however small. Thank God for the good work He has begun.

v: For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land;
o: Thirty days ago, we began in the wilderness, looking for a new thing to spring forth. Today, we end in a garden.
w: Open the note you tucked inside the back cover on Day 2 and the paper you set aside on Day 20. Read them again. Write beside each one what has changed, even a little. Then buy yourself flowers. You have earned them.
